scimon.text: Which material can be used for superconducting properties, and why?

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline Tb-free refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix (VNb)0.753(TiHf)0.247, prepared from ≥99.9% pure elemental ingots; the as-cast matrix is predominantly bcc with slight Nb-rich/Nb-poor segregation.
hidden_target.intervention: Tb was introduced to form (VNb)0.67(TiTbHf)0.33 (HEA-Tb), which was compared directly with the Tb-free matrix. Both alloys were arc-melted under Ti-gettered Ar and remelted five times; nominal mass loss was about 0.8% for HEA-Tb and below 0.2% for the reference.
hidden_target.conditions: As-obtained alloys were characterized by powder XRD/Rietveld refinement and SEM-EDXS. AC susceptibility was measured under zero-field cooling from 1.8–6 K in fields up to 50 kOe, and heat capacity was measured from room temperature to 1.8 K in fields up to approximately 5–6 T. Upper critical fields were derived from field-dependent heat-capacity transitions using the dirty-limit WHH model.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: The Tb-containing alloy retained a bcc HEA matrix with a slightly enlarged lattice parameter, 3.2642(1) Å versus 3.2568(1) Å, indicating some Tb incorporation, but also contained 2.9 wt.% pure-Tb precipitates and 1.7 wt.% Tb2O3, plus a probable Tb concentration gradient near matrix/precipitate interfaces. These nonsuperconducting secondary phases reduce the effective superconducting volume.
hidden_target.mechanism: Tb incorporation and Tb/Tb2O3 inclusions are associated with a broadened superconducting transition and reduced superconducting robustness. The inclusions likely act mainly as nonsuperconducting regions rather than effective flux-pinning centers; any pinning enhancement was weak or negligible. The paper could not determine whether the degradation arises from Tb's intrinsic magnetism or changes in electronic structure, and no magnetic ordering signal attributable to the bulk alloy was detected.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to the Tb-free matrix, adding Tb lowers rather than improves the superconducting transition temperature and upper critical field, broadens the transition, reduces the normalized heat-capacity jump and superconducting volume/field robustness, and causes superconductivity to disappear at a lower applied field.
hidden_target.baseline: The reference was bcc (VNb)0.753(TiHf)0.247 without Tb or XRD-detectable secondary phases, with Tc = 5.2(1) K by heat capacity, μ0Hc2(0) = 6.8 T, and a sharp bulk superconducting transition that remained observable at 5 T.
hidden_target.boundary: The result applies to the synthesized, as-cast polycrystalline compositions and the measured low-temperature range down to 1.8 K and magnetic fields up to roughly 5–6 T. It does not establish that all lanthanide additions are detrimental or resolve whether intrinsic Tb magnetism or electronic-structure modification is the dominant cause.
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: The decisive comparison used the maxima in the imaginary AC susceptibility χ''(T), equal-entropy analysis of the heat-capacity anomaly, and WHH fits to Tc(H) derived from field-dependent specific heat; XRD/Rietveld and SEM-EDXS identified the structural phases mediating the difference.
hidden_target.actual_result: Both alloys showed bulk type-II superconductivity, but HEA-Tb had Tc = 4.6(1) K by heat capacity (about 4.7 K by susceptibility) versus 5.2(1) K for the matrix, and μ0Hc2(0) = 6.1 T versus 6.8 T. At 5 T the matrix remained superconducting whereas HEA-Tb was paramagnetic. The normalized heat-capacity jump fell from 1.49 to 1.05 and the transition broadened. HEA-Tb also had λel-ph = 0.62 versus 0.68, orbital μ0Hc2 = 7.3(1) versus 7.9(1) T, and spin–orbit-scattering parameter 1.1 versus 1.2. Overall, Tb addition provided no beneficial superconducting effect.
